analysis.one_liner: Bars the EPA from issuing or enforcing methane limits on oil and gas production.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote, dying in committee with no cosponsors after being referred to the Energy and Power subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited the EPA from proposing, finalizing, implementing, or enforcing any Clean Air Act restriction on methane emissions from crude oil production and from natural gas production, processing, transmission, and storage. It would have also specifically blocked the EPA from finalizing a 2015 proposed rule that set methane and smog-forming chemical standards for new and modified oil and gas sources. In short, it would have removed an entire category of oil and gas operations from federal air-pollution rules. The bill never moved past its committee referral and expired when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers, processors, pipeline operators, and storage companies would have gained the most. Federal methane rules require leak detection, equipment upgrades, and repairs that cost money; blocking them would have spared those companies those compliance costs while they continued selling the recovered gas.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas producers and pipeline operators

how_it_helps.text: The bill barred the EPA from proposing, finalizing, implementing, or enforcing any Clean Air Act restriction on methane from the oil and gas source category, covering crude oil production and natural gas production, processing, transmission, and storage.

It specifically prohibited the EPA from finalizing or enforcing the September 2015 proposed rule 'Oil and Natural Gas Sector: Emission Standards for New and Modified Sources,' and any substantially similar rule, sparing companies the cost of meeting those new standards.

analysis.who_pays: Communities near oil and gas wells, processing plants, and pipelines would have borne the cost of continued methane leaks and releases of volatile organic compounds, which contribute to smog and health problems. Everyone would share the cost of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, accelerating climate change. Federal taxpayers would also forgo royalty revenue from captured gas that is currently lost to leaks and venting on public lands.
analysis.who_pays_short: People living near wells and the public

drawbacks.text: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and blocking federal standards would have allowed continued leaks and venting across the entire oil and gas supply chain, from the wellhead to the city gate, worsening climate change.

The proposed rule the bill targeted also set standards for volatile organic compounds, which contribute to ground-level ozone and smog; blocking it would have left air-quality harms near production sites unaddressed at the federal level.

The bill's title referred to consumers, but its actual text contained no provision lowering consumer prices; its sole operative effect was removing emission restrictions, so any consumer benefit would have been indirect at best.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main claimed benefit — lower compliance costs for oil and gas companies, possibly passed through as lower energy prices — was speculative and not written into the bill. The costs were concrete: continued methane emissions driving climate change and continued smog-forming pollution near production communities. The bill was a straightforward removal of a regulatory safeguard for one industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2015, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Fleming introduced the bill on November 17, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, where no further action was taken.
The bill attracted no cosponsors during its entire run in the 114th Congress.
No vote was ever held in either chamber, and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, EPA methane and smog-forming emissions rules for oil and gas facilities were never blocked by this legislation; the public retained the regulatory protections the bill would have removed. No industry gained anything from the bill's fate, since it never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept EPA methane protections

for.name: Rep. John Fleming
for.role: House representative from Louisiana and the bill's sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar EPA methane regulation of oil and gas production; it received no cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral with authority to hold hearings and advance the bill
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill past subcommittee referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote was scheduled

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and no votes were ever taken, so no party split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have exempted the entire oil and gas production chain from federal methane restrictions, saving companies leak-detection and equipment-compliance costs while the public absorbed the pollution. Because methane leaks also waste product, blocking rules would have let companies avoid spending without any guarantee of consumer benefit.

industries.industry: Natural gas pipelines, processing, and storage operators
industries.note: The bill's definition of the regulated category extended through gas processing, transmission, and storage up to the city gate, so midstream companies would have been freed from emission standards as well, at the public's expense in air quality and climate impact.
